content: The Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that the proposed interventions have clear benefits, despite limited available evidence. The GDG provided detailed remarks for all recommendations and good practice statements, which are prominently presented alongside the recommendations in Chapter 3 of the guideline. Users of the guideline are encouraged to refer to these remarks for further context. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends kangaroo mother care (KMC) as routine care for all preterm or low-birth-weight infants. KMC can be initiated either in a healthcare facility or at home and should be provided for 8–24 hours per day, as much as possible. Immediate KMC should begin as soon as possible after birth for preterm or low-birth-weight infants. Preterm or low-birth-weight infants should be fed their mother’s own milk or donor human milk as early as possible, ideally starting on the first day after birth. Infants capable of breastfeeding should be put to the breast as soon as possible after birth. For those unable to breastfeed, expressed mother’s milk should be provided as soon as it becomes available. If the mother’s milk is unavailable, donor human milk should be used whenever possible. In healthcare facilities, scheduled feeding may be considered for preterm infants born before 34 weeks of gestation until discharge, rather than responsive feeding. For infants fed via alternative methods (e.g., gastric tube or cup feeding), feed volumes can be increased by up to 30 mL/kg per day. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for preterm or low-birth-weight infants until six months of age. Enteral iron supplementation is recommended for human milk-fed preterm or low-birth-weight infants not receiving iron from other sources. Enteral zinc supplementation may be considered for those not receiving zinc from other sources. Similarly, enteral vitamin D supplementation may be considered for infants not receiving vitamin D from other sources. Probiotics may be considered for very preterm infants (<32 weeks’ gestation) fed human milk. The application of topical emollients to the body of preterm or low-birth-weight infants may also be considered, though this is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy is recommended for preterm infants with clinical signs of respiratory distress syndrome. CPAP therapy may also be considered immediately after birth for very preterm infants (<32 weeks’ gestation), regardless of respiratory distress. Caffeine is recommended for the treatment of apnea in preterm infants and for extubation in preterm infants born before 34 weeks’ gestation. Caffeine may also be considered for the prevention of apnea in preterm infants born before 34 weeks’ gestation, though this is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. Family involvement in the routine care of preterm or low-birth-weight infants in healthcare facilities is recommended. Families should receive additional support, including education, counseling, and discharge preparation, starting from birth and continuing during follow-up post-discharge. Home visits by trained health workers are recommended to support families in caring for their preterm or low-birth-weight infants. Parental leave and entitlements should address the specific needs of mothers, fathers, and other primary caregivers of preterm or low-birth-weight infants. Globally, the prevalence of prematurity and low birth weight (LBW) ranges from 15% to 20%. In 2015, approximately 20.5 million live births were classified as LBW, with 91% occurring in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), primarily in Southern Asia (48%) and sub-Saharan Africa (24%). Preterm and LBW infants are particularly vulnerable to complications such as impaired respiration, feeding difficulties, growth failure, poor temperature regulation, and infections. They are also at increased risk of developmental disabilities, including cerebral palsy and retinopathy of prematurity, as well as long-term chronic conditions like cardiovascular disease. The survival, health, growth, and neurodevelopment of preterm and LBW infants remain significant concerns in many countries, with slow progress in improvement. This is attributed to the complexities of caring for these vulnerable infants and preventing complications. The care of preterm and LBW infants is a global priority and aligns with initiatives such as the United Nations Every Woman Every Child (EWEC) Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health (2016–2030), the UNICEF Every Child Alive campaign, the WHO 2025 global nutrition targets, and the joint WHO–UNICEF Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP) to end preventable deaths. The recommendations in this guideline aim to inform national and subnational health policies, clinical protocols, and programmatic guides. The target audience includes policymakers, healthcare facility managers, health workers (e.g., midwives, nurses, pediatricians, neonatologists), non-governmental organizations, professional societies, academic researchers, and those involved in the education of parents. The guideline includes 25 recommendations and one good practice statement, with 11 new and 14 updated recommendations. Of these, 11 are strong recommendations applicable to all preterm or LBW infants, while 14 are conditional based on specific contexts or conditions. Sixteen recommendations focus on preventive and promotive care, six address care for complications, and three emphasize family involvement and support. A good practice statement was made regarding parental leave and entitlements, recognizing their clear benefits despite limited evidence. The guideline development process followed WHO’s standard operating procedures, including identifying priority questions, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination and implementation. The process involved multiple groups, including the WHO Steering Group, the Guideline Development Group (GDG), the External Review Group (ERG), and the Evidence Synthesis Team (EST). External partners and observers, such as UNICEF and Save the Children, were also involved in the process. All contributors declared potential conflicts of interest, which were reviewed and managed according to WHO guidelines. No declared interests were deemed significant enough to compromise the guideline development process or its credibility.
